title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was deployed to create a fake news article impersonating a real journalist and a public official in order to lend credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated article presented a fictional interview between Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler as if it were real reporting. This deployment had no human editorial review that would have caught the false claims before publication.

This is part of a broader pattern in which AI tools are used to generate convincing impersonations of well-known Australians for investment scams. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports a sharp rise in such schemes, alongside increases in phishing scams and fake investment platforms. It is not established whether a single AI system or service enabled all these incidents, or what technical measures might have prevented the creation and distribution of the fake article.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock having a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article was fabricated and the interview never occurred. This represents a growing category of scam using artificial intelligence to create convincing fake content featuring well-known Australians. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that such schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent.

ASIC data reveals a significant rise in investment scams, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent with 5,476 removed, while fake investment platforms increased 151 percent with 7,051 taken down. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most frequently impersonated public figures. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently and avoid investments from unverifiable sources. Alan Kohler has called for heavy fines against platforms and AI models enabling these scams.
